union.text: northern Zhejiang, the Kuaiji of Xiang Liang

land.text: the Chu rebels' land of 208-207: Cliopatria's 208 shape plus Kuaiji in northern Zhejiang

predecessors.note: The rebel Chu of 208-207 (King Huai II, set up by Xiang Liang) is the same state as Xiang Yu's Western Chu of 206: Cliopatria carries it as one row from 208, and the Xiang Yu page has Xiang Yu 'promoted King Huai II' to Emperor Yi in the spring of 206, and he took the title Hegemon-King of Western Chu. Chu itself (ea-01 chu) ended in 223.

land.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

successors.note: Xiang Yu page: 'After Xiang Yu's death, the rest of Western Chu surrendered and China was unified under Liu Bang's rule'; its infobox names Han Xin as King of Chu as the successor.

capitals.name: Xuyi
capitals.note: King Huai II's seat until Xiang Liang's death at Dingtao in August 208: 'relocated King Huai II from Xuyi to a new capital in Pengcheng'. Coordinates are the modern Xuyi, not on the page.

capitals.name: Pengcheng (Xuzhou)
capitals.note: 'with his kingdom's capital at Pengcheng' (present-day Xuzhou, Jiangsu). It fell to Liu Bang's coalition in September-October 205 and was retaken; the page gives no date for a move.

rulers.name: King Huai II of Chu (Mi Xin)
rulers.title: King of Chu; Emperor Yi of Chu from 206
rulers.note: 'In 208 BC, Xiang Liang installed Mi Xin as King Huai II of Chu'; 'In the spring of 206 BC, Xiang Yu promoted King Huai II' to Emperor Yi, a figurehead, who was assassinated by Ying Bu: 206 on the Timeline page, 205 on the Xiang Yu page.

rulers.name: Xiang Yu
rulers.title: Hegemon-King of Western Chu
rulers.note: Infobox '206-202 BC'; he died c. January 202 BC.

union.text: northern Zhejiang, the Kuaiji of Xiang Liang

correction.text: the Chu rebels' land of 208-207: Cliopatria's 208 shape plus Kuaiji in northern Zhejiang

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 208-207 shape is 201,467 km2 (1,008 grid cells: Jiangsu 505, Anhui 256, Henan 139, Shandong 78) and has one cell of Zhejiang. The Kuaiji page has Xiang Liang taking the commandery in 209 and governing it 209-208 as 'a base for their own rebellion', which 'restored a puppet king to Chu', so northern Zhejiang is added (the 141 Zhejiang cells Cliopatria gives the 206 shape; Cliopatria leaves it in the Qin remnant). No page gives an area or boundary for the 208 Chu.

The Eighteen Kingdoms table gives Western Chu 'Jiangsu, northern Anhui, northern Zhejiang, and eastern and southern Henan'; Cliopatria's 206-204 shape (217,084 km2) holds 96 percent of Jiangsu, 30 percent of Anhui, 141 Zhejiang cells and 128 Henan cells, which agrees. The page has no area. The Xiang Yu page adds only that he 'ruled nine commanderies in the former Liang and Chu states' without naming them.

correction.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

keyframe_review.note: Shape unchanged (354,296 km2: Cliopatria adds 412 of Jiujiang's 429 cells and 468 of Linjiang's 980 to the 206 shape); the years change. It holds 203 and the first month of 202: the Treaty of Hong Canal ('By 203 BC') 'divided China into east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control', and Xiang Yu died c. January 202 ('29 Dec 203 BC to 27 Jan 202 BC'), when 'the rest of Western Chu surrendered'. No page names the boundary, and none dates the Jiujiang and Linjiang cells joining Chu.

union.text: northern Zhejiang, the Kuaiji of Xiang Liang

region.text: the Chu rebels' land of 208-207: Cliopatria's 208 shape plus Kuaiji in northern Zhejiang

ledger.note: 208: Xiang Liang sets up King Huai II of Chu. 'In 208 BC, Xiang Liang installed Mi Xin as King Huai II of Chu', 'wanting to revive the Chu state with the exiled King Huai II as its nominal ruler' (Chu-Han Contention page). The year is the page's; the land is Cliopatria's 208 shape with Kuaiji.

208: the Chu court moves from Xuyi to Pengcheng. 'In the fallout of the defeat, Xiang Yu and Liu Bang relocated King Huai II from Xuyi to a new capital in Pengcheng', after Xiang Liang was 'defeated and killed in action at Dingtao by Zhang Han' in August 208.

206: Xiang Yu declares himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu. Timeline page, 206 BC: 'Xiang Yu divides the former Qin Empire into the Eighteen Kingdoms', 'Xiang Yu declares himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu', 'King Huai II of Chu becomes a figurehead emperor (Emperor Yi of Chu) and gets relocated to Chen County'. The Xiang Yu page has the promotion in the spring of 206.

206: Xiang Yu keeps the Henan lands for Western Chu. The Eighteen Kingdoms table gives Western Chu 'eastern and southern Henan'; the wei dossier (ea-01) records the matching loss. The region is the Henan part of Cliopatria's 206 shape.
205: Liu Bang's coalition takes Pengcheng. 'In September-October 205 BCE, the Chu capital, Pengcheng... fell to a coalition force led by Liu Bang' (Chu-Han Contention page).

205: Xiang Yu retakes Pengcheng. 'Upon hearing this, Xiang Yu turned back from Qi and led 30,000 troops to attack Liu Bang', 'defeating and inflicting heavy casualties on the latter's forces' (Xiang Yu page, which does not state the year or season; the same-year reading follows the Chu-Han Contention page).

204: the Xingyang and Chenggao standoff. Timeline page, 204 BC: 'Xiang Yu attacks Liu Bang's supply lines in Xingyang and Aocang' and 'Xiang Yu defeats Peng Yue, conquers Xingyang, and besieges Liu Bang in Chenggao'.

203: the Treaty of Hong Canal ends the standoff. 'By 203 BC, the tide had turned in Liu Bang's favour. Both sides ultimately agreed to make peace in an event known as the Treaty of Hong Canal', which 'divided China into east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'. The Chu-Han Contention page puts the ceasefire in its 'late 204 BCE' passage; neither gives a boundary.

203: Cliopatria's 203 shape holds Jiujiang. Page silent: the Xiang Yu page does not mention Ying Bu's defection to Liu Bang or Xiang Yu's attack on Jiujiang. The land is the 412 cells of Cliopatria's Jiujiang row inside the 203 shape; the jiujiang dossier should carry the matching loss.

region.text: the eastern part of the Linjiang lands

ledger.note: 203: Cliopatria's 203 shape holds half of Linjiang. Page silent on Gong Wei and Linjiang. The land is the 468 cells of Cliopatria's Linjiang row inside the 203 shape.

region.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

ledger.note: 203: Liu Bang turns on Xiang Yu. Chu-Han Contention page: 'In December 203 BCE, Liu Bang, Han Xin and Peng Yue attacked Xiang Yu from three directions' and trapped him at Gaixia; the Timeline page puts Gaixia in 202. The kingdom-of-han dossier (ea-01) has Liu Bang renouncing the peace in 203.

region.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

ledger.note: 202: Xiang Yu dies. He died c. January 202 BC ('12th month of the 5th year of Liu Bang's reign', converted by the page to 29 Dec 203 BC to 27 Jan 202 BC), trapped 'at Gaixia' and then at the Wu River: 'Xiang Yu then committed suicide by slitting his throat with his sword.' Counterpart han-dynasty: the kingdom-of-han dossier ends in 203 and hands its realm to han-dynasty.

region.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

ledger.note: 202: the rest of Western Chu surrenders to Liu Bang. 'After Xiang Yu's death, the rest of Western Chu surrendered and China was unified under Liu Bang's rule.'

region.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

ledger.note: 202: Western Chu ends with Xiang Yu. Infobox title 'Hegemon-King of Western Chu: 206-202 BC'; successor in the infobox: Han Xin as King of Chu, a Han vassal kingdom.

wars.name: Battle of Pengcheng
wars.outcome: Pengcheng fell to Liu Bang's coalition in September-October 205 and was retaken by Xiang Yu with 30,000 men; the coalition was beaten.
wars.note: The Xiang Yu page gives Liu Bang 'a 560,000-strong army'; the Timeline page lists 'Battle of Pengcheng: Dong Yi and Sima Xin defect to Xiang Yu' under 205.

wars.name: Xiang Yu's campaign against Tian Rong
wars.outcome: Tian Rong, who had seized the Qi lands, retreated to Pingyuan and died there (Timeline, 205); Xiang Yu turned back when Liu Bang took Pengcheng.
wars.note: The Xiang Yu page says Tian Rong 'seized control of the former Qi territories' some months after late 206.

wars.name: Chu-Han Contention

zones.text: Xiang Yu's Western Chu after the Hong Canal agreement: the east, 'Chu' side of 'east and west under Xiang Yu and Liu Bang's control'

wars.outcome: Liu Bang won: the Hong Canal peace of 203 divided the empire east and west, Liu Bang broke it, and Xiang Yu died at Gaixia c. January 202.
wars.note: Dates differ by one year across the pages: Gaixia is 'December 203 BCE' on the Chu-Han Contention page, 202 on the Timeline, and the Xiang Yu page converts the 12th month of the 5th year to 29 Dec 203 BC-27 Jan 202 BC.

certainty.note: No page names a boundary of the Chu lands; the Hong Canal line of 203 is named only as east and west.

notes: One state for the rebel Chu (King Huai II, 208-207) and Xiang Yu's Western Chu (206-202): Cliopatria has them as one row from 208 and the Xiang Yu page treats the title as taken over; chu (ea-01) is the Warring States Chu to 223 and is not this state. The 208-207 shape is a rebel kingdom against Qin (rule 5); it is kept type state because it continues as Western Chu. Cliopatria ends the row in 203; the pages end it in January 202 (Xiang Yu's death), so the 203 shape is extended one year. Disagreements between pages (all one year): Emperor Yi's assassination 206 (Timeline) or 205 (Xiang Yu); Gaixia 'December 203 BCE' (Chu-Han Contention), 202 (Timeline) or c. January 202 (Xiang Yu); Pengcheng 205 (all); Hong Canal 'By 203' (Xiang Yu) or the 'late 204' passage (Chu-Han Contention). Not on any page: the nine commanderies, the Hong Canal line, Ying Bu's defection and Xiang Yu's retaking of Jiujiang (the two gains of 203 are confidence 1), Gong Wei, the date Chu took northern Zhejiang, an infobox area. Counterparts: kingdom-of-han is the ea-01 dossier of Liu Bang's Han; jiujiang, linjiang, wei, qi, han-dynasty are other dossiers. Pages beyond the three shared hubs (Eighteen Kingdoms, Chu-Han Contention, Timeline): Xiang Yu and Kuaiji Commandery, 2 against a budget of 1-2. Gazetteer: all names resolve (Xuzhou and Zhengzhou stand for Pengcheng and Xingyang; Pengcheng, Xuyi and Xingyang are not in places.jsonl).
